cultivar: Anhua and other Hunan medium- and large-leaf population bushes
processing: Post-fermented and pressed: grade-2 to 3 Anhua hei mao cha (pan-fired, rolled, pile-fermented and pine-fire dried) is steamed and pressed into bricks whose faces carry a decorative floral border, then slowly dried; no golden-flower step.
harvest_season: Spring and summer pickings of moderately mature leaf, a grade finer than Hei Zhuan; season is secondary to grade.
appearance_dry: A firm dark-brown brick, usually 1 or 2 kg, with raised flower-pattern borders and characters on the face.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaves with some stems, a little finer and more even than black brick.
taste_profile: Sweet and fairly thick with pine smoke, wood and dried longan, cleaner and rounder than Hei Zhuan, with a cooling finish that grows with age.

brewing.notes: Pry, rinse twice, boiling water, patient late steeps; or simmer 10 g per litre for 5 minutes. Keep the brick wrapped and away from kitchen smells.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year and factory as 1–2 kg bricks; market lots run 1–15 years, drinkable young and preferred by most drinkers at 3–10 years once the smoke has softened. Older bricks from the 1980s–90s are collectables.
description:
Hua Zhuan is the brick that stands in for the famous Anhua log. The Baishaxi factory dates China's first flower brick to 1958, and the usual story says that the thousand-tael log (Qian Liang Cha) was so laborious to make that the factory pressed the same kind of leaf into bricks instead; the flower-pattern border on the brick face is said to recall the 'flower roll' name of the log, hence 'flower brick'. It uses a slightly finer leaf than Hei Zhuan and is pressed less brutally, which makes it the friendlier of the two plain Anhua bricks.

The raw material is the usual Anhua hei mao cha – pan-fired, rolled, briefly piled and dried over pine fires – at roughly grade 2 to 3, steamed and pressed into 1 or 2 kg bricks with the decorative face, then slowly dried. There is no golden-flower step; the tea's character comes from the pine smoke, the leaf and the years.

In the cup it is sweet and fairly thick with pine smoke, wood and dried longan, cleaner and rounder than black brick and less mushroomy than Fu Zhuan, with a cooling finish that becomes more obvious as the brick ages; eight or nine steeps after two rinses with boiling water, or a simmered pot. Young bricks are smoky; give them a few years and the smoke becomes a background note under the sweetness.

It is sold by pressing year and factory, and because the market largely overlooks it in favour of Fu Zhuan and the logs it is often the best-value Anhua tea on the shelf. Check for a clean, sweet, smoky dry smell and a firm, unblemished face; if you want a brick to put away, many drinkers find Hua Zhuan shows its progress sooner than Hei Zhuan.

If a sawn disc of Qian Liang is out of your budget, a Hua Zhuan from the same factory is the usual cheaper way into similar leaf.
sources_note: The 1958 origin as a replacement for Qian Liang Cha at Baishaxi and the origin of the 'flower' name follow Chinese tea-history sources.
history:
The Baishaxi factory in Anhua, founded in 1939, counts a brick made in 1958 as China's first flower brick, and that date is the anchor here, though it comes from the factory's own account. The usual story says the brick replaced the thousand-tael log, the rolled tea also called hua juan, because the log took too much labour to make, and that the flower border on the brick face echoes the old name. That reason is undocumented, so it stays a story for now. Baishaxi also lists hua juan among the traditional teas it has kept going.

Reference entries place flower brick among the Hunan bricks with black brick and Fu brick, and name flower brick and green brick as the teas Mongolians especially favour for milk tea. So its documented place is in Mongolian daily drinking as much as on the shelves of Anhua tea drinkers.
